To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

there was a greater degree of earnings equality in Ireland than in the US during the period from the late 1937 to the mid-1950’s; this compression occurred across all sectors of the economy; it was not the result of a shift in the distribution of workers across sectors; it was a result of the greater integration of Ireland with the UK labour market; it was not due to the effects of the Second World War; it was not a result of industrial protection; and it was not a

the degree of integration with British labour markets is the key determinant of the degree of earnings dispersion in Ireland, and that the Irish labour market was more tightly regulated than the British one.
the distribution of earnings in Ireland was relatively equal in 1938, became more unequal during the war and early post-war years, and became more equal again by the mid-1960s.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the impact of the ‘Great Depression’ of the 1930s, the ‘Second World War’ and the ‘post-war boom’ on the changing distribution of income.
the distributional consequences of economic growth in a peripheral, small open economy, and the extent to which it is integrated with the world economy.

how the Irish economy was able to maintain a relatively egalitarian distribution of earnings during an important period in its economic history, and how this may have contributed to the subsequent rise in inequality.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there was a compression of earnings in Ireland during the period, and that this was a general phenomenon across sectors, but the reasons for this are complex and not fully understood.
the Irish labour market was more compressed in the mid-century than the US.
the ‘great compression’ in Ireland was not a ‘great’ one, but rather one which was ‘good enough’.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, despite the lack of data, the distribution of earnings in Ireland in 1937 and 1968 is consistent with the hypothesis that globalization is associated with increased inequality, but only if we accept the notion that the 1937 and the 1968 distributions are representative of the Irish economy in the absence of globalization.
the period of the great compression in the Irish labour market was not as great as that in the US labour market.
the period of the 1930s, 1940s and 1950s was one of relative egalitarianism in Ireland, and this was due to the interaction of a number of factors.
The main takeaway from our work is that
Ireland's experience was quite different from that of the UK and the US during this period, and that this is not easily explained by the standard theories of the distribution of income.
the Irish experience was not exceptional, and that the Irish case can be fruitfully integrated into comparative analysis of the changing distribution of earnings.
the Irish economy was not an outlier in the 1937 to mid-1950 period; the compression of earnings was a global phenomenon.
